# Predicting Credit Card Default

*By Shuheng Gao*

## Now imagine

You are a credit card sales representative at a bank in the middle of nowhere. You sit in a small office, sharing one desk with three of your colleagues.

Your boss has just evaluated your portfolio, and you are COOKED, because 80% of your customers are not paying off their credit cards at all!!! Now there are two options in front of you: keep bearing the sarcastic looks of your colleagues and wait until the day your boss calls you into a one-on-one meeting and kicks you out of the banking industry.

**OR**, trust the power of ~~Natural Recursion~~ Machine Learning and come back as a legend.

<small>Everyone would choose the second option, right?</small>

However, to save your job using Machine Learning, we first need to identify what kind of problem this is.

In this case, we need to use the known information about our customers to predict whether they will pay off their credit cards before the due date. Thus, we will use the [classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification) technique from [Supervised Learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning) to solve the problem.

## Explore the dataset

Let's take a look at the data the company collected about its customers' credit card payment status.

[Here](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/default-of-credit-card-clients-dataset) is the documentation for the data: you can find the description of every column there and download the dataset to play with if you want.

```{python}
data_set = pd.read_csv("UCI_Credit_Card.csv", index_col="ID")
data_set.head()
```

Do you see any pattern in the first five customers? Of course you don't, because no one can! That's why we need to run a Machine Learning pipeline to find that pattern.

We are relying on the last column of the dataset, `default.payment.next.month`, to tell us whether the customer can pay off their credit card on time.

This column is called the [**target**](https://h2o.ai/wiki/target-variable/). The main goal of our model is to use the data from the rest of the columns to predict the target, so that we can use the result to determine whether we should grant a credit card to a customer. Those columns are called [**features**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feature_(machine_learning)).

Let's look at the histograms of some of the features and their relationship with the target.

```{python}
Image("img/output.png")
```

From the histogram of AGE, we can see that customers aged around 25–30 are more likely to pay on time.

```{python}
Image("img/limitbaloutput.png")
```

From the histogram of LIMIT_BAL, we can see that customers with lower credit limits are more likely to default.

```{python}
Image("img/classdistribution.png")
```

The distribution above shows that the target classes are imbalanced. We will see the effect of that later.

At this stage of a Machine Learning problem, we need to examine more of the dataset to find the hidden pattern linking the target and the features, so that we can apply these findings to later steps of training.

## Model approach

First, let's build a baseline model. Any model we try should outperform the baseline, or it is truly useless (and I mean truly).

The dummy classifier predicts every sample as the majority class.

Hmmmm, it looks like LightGBM has the highest test accuracy. SVC is also doing great, but its training and scoring times are too long, and its F1 score is not ideal. Thus, we will choose LightGBM as our model.

## Final results

With default hyperparameters, the LightGBM model already reaches a test accuracy of 0.819. Do we still have a chance to improve it?

I carried out a hyperparameter optimization and got similar scores:

| Metric | Train | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy | 0.840798 | 0.818524 |
| F1 | 0.541028 | 0.476182 |
| Recall | 0.420328 | 0.369454 |
| Precision | 0.759001 | 0.669862 |
| ROC AUC | 0.867151 | 0.782601 |

*(Fit time: 0.132054 s · Score time: 0.026210 s.)*

What about feature selection?

**RFECV selected 25 features:**

- **Scaled numeric (21):** `LIMIT_BAL`, `AGE`, `PAY_0`, `PAY_2`, `PAY_3`, `PAY_4`, `PAY_6`, `BILL_AMT1`–`BILL_AMT6`, `PAY_AMT1`–`PAY_AMT6`, `DELAY_COUNT`, `MAX_CREDIT_USAGE_RATIO`
- **Ordinal:** `EDUCATION`
- **One-hot:** `SEX_2`, `MARRIAGE_1`, `MARRIAGE_2`

Feature selection with RFECV (recursive feature elimination with cross-validation) shows that LightGBM keeps almost all of the features.

Looks like this is the end of the road for accuracy...

However, we don't evaluate a model's performance by accuracy alone: LightGBM actually has a decent F1 score and recall. This means that the model can identify risky customers for us!

Therefore, although we might reject some new customers who actually could pay off their credit cards, we can use this conservative strategy to improve our performance!

In addition, if our boss is unhappy about rejecting too many customers, we can explain our reasoning by showing the SHAP plot for the customer we rejected.

### Example: why was this customer rejected?

```{python}
Image("img/shapdefault.png")
```

This is a SHAP waterfall plot for a customer who failed to pay off their credit card on time, and our model also correctly predicted the default.

The customer's number of delayed payments during the data-collection months is quite high, which pushes our model toward a positive prediction — the direction of default.

So, the next time your boss asks why we rejected a specific customer, you can use this plot instead of just saying "it's ML magic!"

## Caveats

1. **The effect of class imbalance**

   In the dataset, the ratio of the two target classes is as high as 4:1, which means even the baseline model can give a decent accuracy score. Although we can still use this model considering the improvement in F1 score and recall, the imbalance is still a significant problem that prevents us from achieving better overall performance.

2. **The choice of model**

   Due to compute and time limits of the project, I was not able to try other kinds of models or fine-tune some of them. For example, although KNN and SVC performed almost as well as LightGBM, the training time of the two models makes it hard to fine-tune their hyperparameters. In addition, the dataset is large enough to train a neural network model on, but I was not able to try one.

3. **Limited features in the dataset**

   The features in the dataset consist only of financial data and very limited personal data of the customers. If the dataset were more detailed, with information such as employment, income, and savings status of the customers, the model could consider more variables and might give better outcomes.
